tasks.short: Note what guests say about dishes, report sales and returns, join the menu meeting, taste new dishes and help word the menu card.

steps.what: Servers ring up orders and void dishes sent back to the kitchen in the till
Host notes guests' comments and questions about dishes during service: on a notepad today, as tags against a dish on the host stand's tablet after the change
Host recalls from memory which dishes sold well and which came back
Host confers with the chef and manager to help plan menus
Host tastes new dishes and suggests how to present them to guests
Host helps word the dish descriptions for the menu card

tasks.design: Servers already ring every order in the point-of-sale system ({OTHER}); when a dish comes back they void it with a 'sent back' reason, and the host notes guest comments as tags against a dish on the host stand's tablet instead of a notepad, which takes as long. A scheduled weekly report in the till shows sales per dish, dishes sent back and the tags, which the host reads and adds context to. The menu meeting, tasting and wording stay with the staff.
tasks.previous_blocker: Feedback lived on notepads and in memory.
tasks.enabler_now: Point-of-sale systems record sales per dish and can take simple tags.
tasks.still_hard: Menu choices are taste and people judgements; tags give only part of the story.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing what regulars keep asking for.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes; the host brings facts to the meeting.

reach.learn: Whether sales and return figures change menu decisions.

evidence.claim: Point-of-sale systems report sales per item and can record simple notes.
Allergy notes are health data; record only what the kitchen needs and not with the guest's name in feedback.

assumptions: Boundary: from guest comments to the menu card text; pricing is outside.

Input contract for s2: sales per dish and dishes sent back come from the till records servers make in s6 (returns voided with a 'sent back' reason); comment tags come from the host in s1; dish list and tags set up by the restaurant manager; fallback is notepads.
Coverage: servers record a reason for most but not all returns, so the host still adds what was missed; s2 keeps half its time.
Tags are per dish, not per guest, and returns are not used to rate servers.
The meeting, tasting, wording and noting comments keep their full time; noting is the host's own first record. s2 keeps 50 because the weekly report replaces recalling sales and returns from memory.
research_questions: Do menu changes based on returns cut waste?

already_counted.description: Host checks the weekly dish report against what was seen in service and adds missing returns.

incremental.description: No ongoing upkeep for the host: the dish list and tags are set up and kept by the restaurant manager.
Servers tap a 'sent back' reason when voiding a returned dish.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: servers record a reason for only half of returns and the host fills the gaps from memory, so s2 keeps 75 (3.8); high: most returns carry a reason (7.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Plan posts and offers, write texts, get offers approved, publish posts and the newsletter, hand out flyers and keep listings current.

steps.what: Host plans marketing posts and offers for the month with the manager
Host writes texts for posts, the newsletter and flyers

loop.input: The content plan entry (event, date, offer, price), the restaurant's house style notes and three past posts.
loop.output: A short social post, a newsletter paragraph and a flyer line for that entry.
loop.check: Code checks that every date, time, price and opening hour in the draft matches the content plan and the opening hours record, and that no offer appears that is not in the plan. The host reads each draft against the plan for meaning: what it promises is what the restaurant offers, with its limits; drafts that do not fit are rewritten by hand.
loop.stop: One draft and one redraft; then the host writes it.
loop.why_not_simpler: Each post needs fresh wording; fixed templates read the same every week.

steps.what: Restaurant manager approves the offers and prices in the texts
Host checks the final posts before scheduling: offers, prices and dates as the manager approved, wording, and the channel and time
Host publishes posts on social media
Host checks the final newsletter before sending: offers, prices and dates as approved, wording, and that the list holds only opted-in guests
Host sends the newsletter to guests
Host hands out flyers and talks with local businesses
Restaurant manager decides changed opening hours and passes them to the host
Restaurant manager checks the changed opening hours in the platform before they go to the channels: dates, times and closures
Host updates opening hours on the booking channels one by one
Host checks the listing changes before publishing: opening hours against the platform and menu text against the approved texts
Host updates opening hours and the menu on the website and other listing sites

tasks.design: A bounded step drafts posts, newsletter text and flyer lines from the month's content plan, with code checking dates, prices and hours against the plan; the host reads each draft for meaning and rewrites what does not fit, and the manager approves offers; the host checks each post and newsletter before it goes out. Approved posts are scheduled in a {SOCIAL} tool, and the newsletter goes through {MARKETING_AUTOMATION} to guests who opted in when booking, whose list the reservation platform ({OTHER}) exports to it. The manager enters changed opening hours once in the reservation platform and checks them, and its channel connection updates the booking channels; the website and other listings are still updated by the host, who checks each change before publishing.
tasks.previous_blocker: Each post, mail and listing was written and updated by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Reservation platforms put booking widgets and buttons on the restaurant's site and partner platforms, and keep a central guest database.
tasks.still_hard: Marketing e-mail needs prior consent; the restaurant's voice must stay its own.
tasks.human_edge: Being the friendly face that local businesses and neighbours remember.
tasks.altitude: The host edits drafts and schedules; offers stay the manager's decision.

evidence.claim: A reservation platform puts a booking widget on the restaurant's site and booking buttons on partner platforms, and sends automated reminders.
A reservation manager keeps a central guest database with seating plans.
Marketing e-mail to guests needs their prior consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from planning content to listings updated; paid advertising agencies are outside.

Input contract for s6: opening hours entered by the restaurant manager in the reservation platform (s8, with about the effort of telling the host today); the platform's channel connection is the producer for the booking channels; fallback is the host updating each channel.
Input contract for s7: guests who ticked the newsletter box when booking, exported by the reservation platform to the marketing tool each night; fallback is the host's mailing list.
The website and other listing sites are not connected, so s9 keeps its time.
Manager time is outside the host's savings; flyers and local contacts do not change.

Planning, flyers, the website and listings and every check before a post, newsletter or listing goes out keep their full time. s2 keeps 70 because drafts fill dates and offers but the host still writes for tone and meaning. s4 keeps 60 and s7 keeps 70 because scheduling and the nightly opted-in list replace posting and list work by hand.
unknowns: How many channels the restaurant uses.
Size of the opted-in guest list.
research_questions: Do scheduled posts bring more bookings than ad hoc posts?

incremental.description: Host keeps the content plan current in the drafting tool.
Host checks once a month that the booking channels show the platform's hours.

approvals.approved_version: The month's posts with offers, prices and dates exactly as approved by the manager in s3 and checked by the host in s4c, scheduled once in the {SOCIAL} tool on the named channels; any change needs a new approval and check.

The newsletter text with offers, prices and dates exactly as approved by the manager in s3 and checked by the host in s7c, sent once through {MARKETING_AUTOMATION} to the opted-in guest list; any change needs a new approval and check.

The opening hours with dates, times and closures exactly as checked by the restaurant manager in s8c, sent once by the platform's channel connection to the booking channels; a later change needs a new entry and check.
The opening hours and menu text exactly as checked by the host in s9c, published once on the website and the named listing sites; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: drafts are mostly rewritten and posts are rare, so s2 keeps 90 and s4 keeps 80 (13.3); high: drafts are used and posts are scheduled as designed (21.3).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The host keeps welcoming, tasting and local contacts; notes, posts and listings take less time.
reach: Restaurant managers' menu and promotion decisions
skills_to_grow: Editing drafted posts in the house voice
role.ambitious_version: A host who brings real guest feedback to every menu meeting and keeps the restaurant visible without evenings at a laptop.

job.title: Hosts and Hostesses, Restaurant, Lounge, and Coffee Shop
